tagline: A Piedmont byway, with Orange County’s past in the surrounding landscape
intro: The Scots-Welsh Heritage Byway belongs to North Carolina’s Piedmont group of scenic roads. NCDOT’s byways program selects roads for their historic, geographic and cultural qualities.
In Orange County, Hillsborough developed where the Great Indian Trading Path crossed the Eno River. The town was founded in 1754; its Nash-Hooper House followed in 1772, built by Francis Nash.

Hillsborough stands in central Orange County, while Chapel Hill and Carrboro occupy its southeastern part. Occoneechee Mountain rises beside Hillsborough; Cane Creek Reservoir supplies the Carrboro-Chapel Hill area.

moments.title: Nash-Hooper House
moments.text: Francis Nash built this Hillsborough house in 1772, before his service as a Continental Army general ended with his death at Germantown in 1777. William Hooper, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, bought it in 1782 and lived here until his death in 1790. The wood-frame house has clapboard siding and a high stone foundation. It remains a private residence and is not normally open to the public. Hooper was first buried in the east garden; his remains were moved to Guilford Courthouse in 1894. The house retains original pine floors and some fireplace mantels.

moments.title: Occoneechee Mountain State Natural Area
moments.text: Occoneechee Mountain rises more than 350 feet above the Eno River, reaching Orange County’s highest point. The natural area occupies land settled by the Occaneechi Band of the Saponi Nation. A mill village occupied part of the land until 1987. State park officials began purchasing land here in December 1997. The natural area now covers 221 acres, with more than three miles of trails and a connection to Hillsborough’s paved Riverwalk along the Eno. Brown elfin butterflies live here, separated from the nearest other population by more than 100 miles to the west.

moments.title: Cane Creek Reservoir
moments.text: Cane Creek Reservoir supplies the Carrboro-Chapel Hill area, but its creation cost residents homes and farmland. As population growth outstripped University Lake’s capacity, officials considered a new water source. The Cane Creek Conservation Association opposed the project; the Orange Water and Sewer Authority supported it. Courts compelled landowners to sell watershed property through eminent domain, and the reservoir filled in 1989. The 540-acre reservoir receives water from Cane Creek, Tom’s Creek, Watery Creek and Turkey Hill Creek. The Orange Water and Sewer Authority operates it for the communities it serves.
